newsitem.title: USA: Dole pushes economic plan in midwest.
newsitem.headline: Dole pushes economic plan in midwest.

text.p: Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole brushed aside his low standing in polls on Wednesday and confidently predicted victory over President Bill Clinton based on his economic plan.

Dole flew to Amana, Iowa, for a farm rally at a huge farm equipment show, the Farm Progress Show, which draws 100,000 people daily and expressed a confidence he will be elected even though he lags by double digits in polls.

Dole, from neighbouring Kansas and introduced as "the hero of the heartland," promoted his economic programme based on tax cuts and asked the rally crowd to compare his plan to Clinton's, a focus he believes will get voters to switch to him once they know his programme.
"Take a look at President Clinton's record of high taxes, high spending and a slow growth economy and compare it to our plan," he said.
"Our plan is simply this: you keep more of your freedom, and more money in your pocket or more money in your paycheck ... and get the economy moving," Dole said.
"We've had the slowest growth we've had in a century," Dole said, repeating a claim Clinton disputes by noting the long period of economic expansion.
Dole wound up a two-day campaign trip to Detroit, Shelby, Ohio, St. Louis and Iowa before heading back to Washington and then on to Florida for preparations for presidential debates.
In St. Louis he said he would win the election because he had better ideas.
And his running mate Jack Kemp went further on a morning television interview, saying overcoming a double-digit lead by Clinton would be "a piece of cake."
Dole was in a fighting mood before about 2,000 students jammed into an auditorium at St. Louis University.

This was supposed to be the date of the first debate between Dole and Clinton at nearby Washington University, but both camps changed the date of the first of two debates to Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and excluded Reform Party candidate Ross Perot from taking part.
The paths of Dole and Perot -- who blames Dole and a bipartisan debate commission for shutting him out of the debates -- crossed in this city.

Perot planned to come to St. Louis University on Wednesday night when he is expected to continue his campaign to get into the debates. Perot also has filed a federal lawsuit in his bid to be a debater.
Dole urged the students here to tune into the debate a week from Sunday so "you'll hear from Bob Dole, the next president of the United States."

A few pro-Perot hecklers were in the college audience, but Dole told his cheering student fans "don't be distracted by the noises here, it's all going to be over and we're going to win, we're going to win because we have the ideas because we have the agenda."
Dole pushed his economic package, centred on a 15 percent income tax cut, a capital gains tax cut and a $500 per child tax credit, at the rally in St. Louis.

This Mississippi River city was in an ecstatic mood since its St. Louis Cardinals baseball team clinched the National League Central Division on Tuesday, the first time the team had won a playoff spot since 1987.
"And there's good reason to celebrate today," Dole said, noting the win by the Cardinals.

He then joked "if I wanted to titillate the press I would have said the St. Louis Browns" -- referring to the city's long departed baseball team in a joke about his comment in California last week when he congratulated a pitcher for the long-gone "Brooklyn Dodgers" for a no-hitter instead of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
